title: Training Deep Neural Networks
subtitle: Diagnose and fix what stops deep networks learning: vanishing and exploding gradients, slow or unstable optimisation, overfitting and badly scaled activations, in TensorFlow and Keras.
outcomes: Diagnose vanishing and exploding gradients from per-layer gradient norms, and fix them with activations, initialisation and clipping
Explain and implement momentum, RMSprop and Adam, and choose and schedule learning rates
Control overfitting with L1 and L2 penalties, weight decay, dropout, data augmentation and early stopping
Use batch normalisation correctly in training and inference, and know when layer normalisation suits better
Debug a training run from its first loss and learning curves, and optimise a deep network for a hold-out test set
prerequisites: Introduction to Neural Networks and TensorFlow: dense networks, backpropagation, and building and training Keras models. Comfortable Python, NumPy and basic calculus. Install Python 3.10 or later, then pip install tensorflow scikit-learn matplotlib (TensorFlow 2.16 or later, with Keras 3). The capstone downloads Fashion-MNIST, about 30 MB, once.
description:
A network that's deep enough to be useful is also deep enough to be hard to train. Its gradients can fade to nothing or blow up on the way back through its layers, plain gradient descent can crawl or bounce, a large model can memorise its training data instead of learning from it, and the scale of its activations can drift as it learns. This course is about the techniques that fix those problems, and about knowing which one a failing network needs.

You'll measure gradients layer by layer and fix them with non-saturating activations, Glorot and He initialisation and gradient clipping; write momentum, RMSprop and Adam yourself and check them against Keras; schedule learning rates with decay and warm-up; regularise with L1 and L2, weight decay, dropout, augmentation and early stopping; and implement batch normalisation by hand before using it in Keras. The last module brings everything together in a training recipe and a debugging routine, and the capstone hands you a deep network that fails on Fashion-MNIST for you to diagnose and rescue, one measured change at a time. Every lab runs on a laptop CPU with fixed seeds and comes with starter code and the output to expect.

modules.title: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
modules.summary: Find out why deep networks are hard to train: measure gradients shrinking or growing layer by layer, see how saturating activations make it worse, and fix it with non-saturating activations, careful initialisation and gradient clipping.

lessons.title: Why gradients vanish or explode
objectives: Explain how backpropagation multiplies one factor per layer
Recognise the symptoms of vanishing and exploding gradients
Measure per-layer gradient norms, and limit exploding ones with clipping
key_points: Backpropagation multiplies the gradient by one factor per layer, made of that layer's weights and its activation's slope, so the gradient reaching the first layer is roughly a product of many factors: below 1 on average and it shrinks exponentially with depth, above 1 and it grows exponentially.

Vanishing gradients show as early layers that barely change, a loss that falls a little and then stalls, and gradient norms that drop layer by layer towards the input: the network trains like a shallow one stacked on near-random features.

Exploding gradients show as a loss that jumps about, overflows to inf or becomes NaN, and weights that grow huge. Recurrent networks are especially prone, because the same weights multiply the gradient at every time step.
Measure rather than guess: run one batch through a tf.GradientTape, take the gradient for each layer's kernel, and compare their norms (tf.norm) from the first layer to the last.

Gradient clipping limits the damage when gradients explode: Keras optimisers take clipnorm (rescale each variable's gradient to at most that norm), global_clipnorm (all gradients together) or clipvalue (cap each element). It treats the symptom; initialisation and normalisation treat the cause.

lessons.title: Saturating and non-saturating activations
objectives: Explain why sigmoid and tanh make vanishing gradients worse
Compare ReLU, leaky ReLU, ELU, SELU and GELU
Choose a hidden-layer activation for a deep network
key_points: The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so every sigmoid layer cuts the gradient by a factor of at least 4 before the weights act, and saturated units pass back almost nothing; its outputs are also always positive, which skews the next layer's updates. tanh is centred on 0 but saturates too.

ReLU's slope is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so gradients pass through active units undiminished. Units whose input stays below 0 have slope 0 and never recover (dead ReLUs), which a learning rate that's too high or a large negative bias can cause.

Leaky ReLU, max(αz, z), keeps a small slope for negative inputs: Keras's LeakyReLU layer defaults to α = 0.3 (negative_slope), but keras.activations.leaky_relu to 0.2. ELU, α(e^z − 1) below 0, is smooth and pulls the mean activation towards 0; Keras's alpha defaults to 1.0.

SELU scales ELU so that, with LeCun normal initialisation and a plain stack of Dense layers, activations keep a mean near 0 and a variance near 1 by themselves (self-normalising networks, Klambauer et al., 2017); regular dropout breaks this, so such networks use AlphaDropout.

GELU, z·Φ(z) with Φ the standard normal's cumulative distribution, is a smooth ReLU-like curve used in transformers such as BERT and GPT; Swish (SiLU), z·σ(z), is similar. ReLU remains a sound default, and GELU or Swish are worth trying.

lessons.title: Weight initialisation: Glorot, He and LeCun
objectives: Explain how the initial weights' scale sets the variance of activations and gradients
Choose Glorot, He or LeCun initialisation to suit an activation
Set initialisers on Keras layers
key_points: A unit sums fan_in weighted inputs, so with zero-mean weights of variance σ² and inputs of variance v, its weighted sum has a variance of about fan_in·σ²·v. Unless fan_in·σ² is about 1 (adjusted for the activation), activations grow or shrink by that factor at every layer, and gradients do the same on the way back.

Glorot (Xavier) initialisation (Glorot and Bengio, 2010) uses Var(W) = 2/(fan_in + fan_out), a compromise between steady forward and backward variances, suited to tanh, sigmoid and softmax layers. glorot_uniform, drawn from ±√(6/(fan_in + fan_out)), is the default for Keras's Dense layers, with biases at 0.

He initialisation (He et al., 2015) uses Var(W) = 2/fan_in to make up for ReLU zeroing about half its inputs: kernel_initializer="he_normal" (a truncated normal in Keras) or "he_uniform" for ReLU-family layers. LeCun initialisation, Var(W) = 1/fan_in ("lecun_normal"), goes with SELU.

Weights that are too large saturate sigmoid and tanh units or blow up ReLU activations; weights that are too small make the signal fade layer by layer; and identical weights never break the symmetry between units.

Initialisation matters most in deep plain stacks. Batch normalisation (Module 4) and residual connections make networks much less sensitive to it, but a suitable initialiser is still the right starting point.

"""Measure each layer's gradient in a deep network, see gradients vanish and explode, and fix them."""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

DEPTH, WIDTH = 10, 64


def load_data():
    X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
    X = X.astype("float32") / 16.0
    return train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)


def deep_mlp(activation, initializer):
    """DEPTH hidden layers of WIDTH units, then a 10-way softmax."""
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(64,))])
    for _ in range(DEPTH):
        model.add(layers.Dense(WIDTH, activation=activation, kernel_initializer=initializer))
    model.add(layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"))
    return model


def kernel_gradient_norms(model, X, y):
    """The L2 norm of the loss gradient for each Dense layer's kernel, first layer first."""
    loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()
    # TODO: inside a tf.GradientTape, run the model on X and compute the loss; then get the gradients of the
    #      loss for each Dense layer's kernel (layer.kernel) and return their norms (tf.norm) as a list of floats
    return [1.0] * len(model.layers)


def verdict(norms):
    """Exploding if any gradient is huge; vanishing if the first layer's is tiny next to the output layer's."""
    if max(norms) > 1e2:
        return "exploding"
    if norms[0] / norms[-1] < 1e-2:
        return "vanishing"
    return "healthy"


def main():
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = load_data()
    batch_X, batch_y = X_train[:256], y_train[:256]
    configs = {
        "sigmoid + glorot_uniform": ("sigmoid", "glorot_uniform"),
        "tanh + glorot_uniform": ("tanh", "glorot_uniform"),
        "relu + he_normal": ("relu", "he_normal"),
        "relu + normal(stddev=0.5)": ("relu", keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=0.5)),
    }
    print(f"Gradient norms in a {DEPTH}-layer MLP on one batch of 256 digits")
    print(f"{'configuration':28} {'layer 1':>9} {'layer 5':>9} {'layer 10':>9} {'output':>9}  first/output  verdict")
    for name, (activation, init) in configs.items():
        norms = kernel_gradient_norms(deep_mlp(activation, init), batch_X, batch_y)
        ratio = norms[0] / norms[-1]
        print(f"{name:28} {norms[0]:9.2e} {norms[4]:9.2e} {norms[9]:9.2e} {norms[10]:9.2e}  {ratio:12.1e}  {verdict(norms)}")

    print("\nTraining each for 10 epochs with SGD(learning_rate=0.05)")
    for name, (activation, init) in configs.items():
        model = deep_mlp(activation, init)
        model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.05),
                      loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
        history = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=32, verbose=0)
        loss = history.history["loss"][-1]
        acc = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=0)[1]
        print(f"{name:28} final training loss {loss:9.3f}   test accuracy {acc:.3f}")

    print("\nThe exploding network again, with gradient clipping (clipnorm=1.0)")
    # TODO: compile deep_mlp("relu", keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=0.5)) with
    #      keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.05, clipnorm=1.0), train it the same way and print the same line


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: layer.kernel is a Dense layer's weight matrix; model.layers lists the Dense layers in order, the output layer last.
model(X, training=True) runs the model the way fit() does; gradients come from the tape only for computations inside its with block.
Exact norms vary a little between machines; the verdicts and their orders of magnitude are what matter.

modules.title: Advanced Optimisers
modules.summary: Go beyond plain stochastic gradient descent: momentum and Nesterov, the adaptive methods AdaGrad, RMSprop and Adam, decoupled weight decay with AdamW, and learning-rate schedules with warm-up.

lessons.title: Momentum and Nesterov
objectives: Explain why plain SGD struggles on ill-conditioned losses
Write the momentum update and explain what β controls
Use SGD with momentum and Nesterov in Keras
key_points: Plain SGD steps along the negative mini-batch gradient. On a ravine-shaped (ill-conditioned) loss, steep across and shallow along, a learning rate small enough for the steep direction makes painfully slow progress along the shallow one, and a larger one zig-zags or diverges across it.

Momentum keeps a velocity: v ← βv − η∇L, then w ← w + v, with β usually 0.9. Gradients that keep pointing the same way build up speed, up to 1/(1 − β) = 10 times a single step, while components that flip sign from step to step cancel out.

That built-up speed carries the weights across flat regions, saddle points and small dips in the loss; in high-dimensional networks, plateaus and saddle points are thought to slow training more than poor local minima do.

Nesterov momentum takes the gradient at the look-ahead point w + βv, where the velocity is about to carry the weights, so it corrects overshooting sooner: keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True).
Momentum makes the effective step larger, so a learning rate that suits plain SGD is often too large with momentum: tune the two together.

lessons.title: Adaptive learning rates: AdaGrad, RMSprop and Adam
objectives: Explain how AdaGrad, RMSprop and Adam scale each parameter's step
Describe Adam's bias correction
Choose between Adam, AdamW and SGD with momentum
key_points: AdaGrad divides each parameter's step by the square root of the sum of its squared gradients, so rarely updated parameters take larger steps; but the sum only grows, so the effective learning rate shrinks towards 0 and training can stall.
RMSprop, proposed by Geoffrey Hinton in a lecture course, swaps the sum for a moving average, s ← ρs + (1 − ρ)g², and steps by ηg/(√s + ε). Keras's defaults are ρ = 0.9, η = 0.001 and ε = 10⁻⁷.

Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) keeps a moving average of the gradients (momentum, β1 = 0.9) and of their squares (as RMSprop, β2 = 0.999), and divides each by 1 − β^t at step t to correct their bias towards 0 early on; Keras's default learning rate for it is 0.001.

Because adaptive methods divide by the gradient's typical size, their steps are about η whatever the gradient's scale, so they need less tuning and make fast early progress; with a constant η they hover around a minimum rather than settling exactly, which is one reason to decay the rate.

With Adam, an L2 penalty in the loss isn't the same as weight decay, because the penalty's gradient is rescaled too. AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter) decays the weights separately: keras.optimizers.AdamW, whose weight_decay defaults to 0.004. Well-tuned SGD with momentum remains common, notably for image classifiers.

lessons.title: Learning-rate schedules and warm-up
objectives: Explain why the learning rate is changed during training
Set up step, exponential and cosine schedules and ReduceLROnPlateau in Keras
Find a starting learning rate with a range test
key_points: The learning rate is usually the most important setting: start high enough to make fast progress, then lower it so the weights settle into a minimum instead of bouncing around it.

Keras schedules are functions of the optimiser's step count (batches, not epochs), passed as learning_rate: PiecewiseConstantDecay steps down at set boundaries, ExponentialDecay(initial, decay_steps, decay_rate) multiplies by decay_rate every decay_steps, and CosineDecay follows a half cosine down to a floor.

Warm-up starts with a small learning rate and raises it over the first few hundred or thousand steps, which steadies Adam's early estimates and large-batch training, and is standard for transformers; CosineDecay does it with warmup_target and warmup_steps.

Callbacks can change the rate between epochs instead: ReduceLROnPlateau(monitor="val_loss", factor=0.5, patience=3) halves it when validation loss stops improving, and LearningRateScheduler(function) sets it from the epoch number.

A learning-rate range test (Leslie Smith) trains briefly while raising the rate exponentially, say from 10⁻⁶ to 1, and plots the loss against the rate: choose a rate somewhat below the point where the loss falls fastest, well before it starts to climb.

"""Optimisers from scratch on a ravine-shaped loss, checked against Keras, then compared on a real network."""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

CURVATURE = np.array([1.0, 50.0])  # loss = 0.5 * (1 * w1^2 + 50 * w2^2): steep across, shallow along


def loss(w):
    return 0.5 * float(np.sum(CURVATURE * w ** 2))


def grad(w):
    return CURVATURE * w


def sgd(w, g, state, lr):
    return w - lr * g


def momentum(w, g, state, lr, beta=0.9):
    # TODO: keep a velocity in state["v"] (start at zeros): v = beta * v - lr * g, then return w + v
    return w


def rmsprop(w, g, state, lr, rho=0.9, eps=1e-7):
    # TODO: keep a moving average of squared gradients in state["s"]: s = rho * s + (1 - rho) * g**2,
    #      then return w - lr * g / (sqrt(s) + eps)
    return w


def adam(w, g, state, lr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-7):
    # TODO: count steps in state["t"]; m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g; v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * g**2;
    #      correct the bias: m_hat = m / (1 - beta1**t), v_hat = v / (1 - beta2**t);
    #      return w - lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps)
    return w


def losses_after(step, lr, checkpoints=(100, 300), start=(-4.0, 2.0)):
    """Run an optimiser from start; return the loss at each checkpoint, or "diverged"."""
    w, state, out = np.array(start), {}, []
    for i in range(1, max(checkpoints) + 1):
        w = step(w, grad(w), state, lr)
        if not np.isfinite(w).all() or loss(w) > 1e6:
            return ["diverged"] * len(checkpoints)
        if i in checkpoints:
            out.append(f"{loss(w):.1e}")
    return out


def check_against_keras(lr=0.1, steps=5):
    """Run our adam() and keras.optimizers.Adam side by side on the same loss."""
    w_ours, state = np.array([-4.0, 2.0]), {}
    w_keras = tf.Variable([-4.0, 2.0], dtype=tf.float64)
    opt = keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        w_ours = adam(w_ours, grad(w_ours), state, lr)
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            l = 0.5 * tf.reduce_sum(tf.constant(CURVATURE) * w_keras ** 2)
        opt.apply_gradients([(tape.gradient(l, w_keras), w_keras)])
    return w_ours, w_keras.numpy()


def compare_on_digits():
    X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
    X = X.astype("float32") / 16.0
    X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)
    steps_per_epoch = int(np.ceil(len(X_train) / 32))
    optimizers = {
        "SGD lr=0.01": lambda: keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01),
        "SGD + momentum 0.9": lambda: keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9),
        "SGD + Nesterov": lambda: keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9, nesterov=True),
        "RMSprop lr=0.001": lambda: keras.optimizers.RMSprop(learning_rate=0.001),
        "Adam lr=0.001": lambda: keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
        "Adam + cosine decay": lambda: keras.optimizers.Adam(
            learning_rate=keras.optimizers.schedules.CosineDecay(0.003, decay_steps=15 * steps_per_epoch)),
    }
    print(f"\nA 3 x 128 ReLU network on the digits, 15 epochs each ({steps_per_epoch} steps per epoch)")
    for name, make in optimizers.items():
        keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
        model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(64,))] +
                                 [layers.Dense(128, activation="relu", kernel_initializer="he_normal") for _ in range(3)] +
                                 [layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")])
        model.compile(optimizer=make(), loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
        h = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=15, batch_size=32, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), verbose=0).history
        print(f"{name:22} val_loss after 1 epoch {h['val_loss'][0]:.3f}, after 15 {h['val_loss'][-1]:.3f}; "
              f"val_accuracy {h['val_accuracy'][-1]:.3f}")


def main():
    print("Loss after 100 and 300 steps from w = (-4, 2) on loss = 0.5 * (w1^2 + 50 * w2^2)")
    trials = [("SGD", sgd, 0.01), ("SGD", sgd, 0.039), ("SGD", sgd, 0.041), ("Momentum", momentum, 0.02),
              ("RMSprop", rmsprop, 0.03), ("RMSprop", rmsprop, 0.1), ("Adam", adam, 0.1)]
    for name, step, lr in trials:
        after_100, after_300 = losses_after(step, lr)
        print(f"{name:9} lr={lr:<6} after 100 steps: {after_100:9}  after 300 steps: {after_300}")
    ours, theirs = check_against_keras()
    print("Our Adam after 5 steps:", ours.round(6), " keras.optimizers.Adam:", theirs.round(6))
    print("Our Adam matches Keras:", bool(np.allclose(ours, theirs, atol=1e-6)))
    compare_on_digits()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Regularisation Strategies
modules.summary: Stop deep networks memorising their training data: penalise large weights with L1 and L2, drop units at random, stop training at the right moment, and create more training data with augmentation.

lessons.title: Weight penalties: L1, L2 and weight decay
objectives: Explain how L1 and L2 penalties change what a network learns
Add regularisers to Keras layers and read the penalty they add
Distinguish L2 regularisation from decoupled weight decay
key_points: L2 regularisation adds λΣw² to the loss and pulls every weight smoothly towards 0; L1 adds λΣ|w| and pushes many weights to exactly 0, giving a sparse model. Both favour simpler functions that are less able to memorise noise.

In Keras a penalty goes on a layer, Dense(256, kernel_regularizer=keras.regularizers.L2(1e-4)), and model.losses lists the penalty terms. Keras adds them to the loss that fit() and evaluate() report, so compare models with and without penalties on metrics or on the plain loss.
Keras's L2(l2) adds l2 × Σw², with no factor of ½, so its gradient is 2·l2·w; libraries and papers define the factor differently, so a λ copied from elsewhere may need adjusting.

With plain SGD an L2 penalty is equivalent to weight decay, shrinking every weight by a constant fraction each step; with adaptive optimisers it isn't, which is why AdamW applies weight decay separately from the gradient.
Penalise kernels, not biases or batch normalisation's parameters, and tune λ on validation data: too small does nothing and too large makes the network underfit.

lessons.title: Dropout
objectives: Explain how dropout behaves in training and at inference
Add dropout to a Keras model and choose a rate
Use Monte Carlo dropout to estimate uncertainty
key_points: Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) sets each unit's output to 0 with probability p, the rate, at every training step, and scales the surviving outputs by 1/(1 − p) (inverted dropout) so that each unit's expected output is unchanged.
At inference nothing is dropped. Keras's Dropout layer acts only when the model runs with training=True, as it does inside fit(); predict() and evaluate() leave it off.
Because any unit may disappear, units can't rely on particular partners (co-adaptation), and training resembles averaging a huge ensemble of thinned networks that share their weights.
Typical rates are 0.1 to 0.5, higher for wide dense layers. With dropout the training loss is higher and noisier than without, and training takes more epochs, so judge it on validation metrics.

Monte Carlo dropout keeps dropout on at prediction time, model(x, training=True), and averages many passes; the spread of those predictions gives a rough measure of the model's uncertainty (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016).

lessons.title: Early stopping and data augmentation
objectives: Configure early stopping so that it keeps the best weights
Choose label-preserving augmentations and apply them with Keras layers
Name other regularisers, such as label smoothing
key_points: Early stopping treats the number of epochs as a setting chosen on validation data: EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=10, restore_best_weights=True) stops after 10 epochs without improvement and returns to the best weights. restore_best_weights defaults to False, which keeps the last, worse, weights.

Data augmentation trains on random, label-preserving changes to each example, such as small shifts, rotations, zooms, flips and contrast changes for images, so the network sees far more variety than the dataset holds.

Keras's preprocessing layers (RandomFlip, RandomRotation, RandomTranslation, RandomZoom, RandomContrast) augment inside the model, only when training=True, so evaluation and prediction see the original images.
An augmentation must not change the right answer: a horizontal flip suits photos of animals but not handwritten digits or text, and rotating a 6 by 180 degrees makes it a 9.

Other regularisers: label smoothing (CategoricalCrossentropy(label_smoothing=0.1), with one-hot labels) stops the network pushing probabilities to exactly 0 and 1, GaussianNoise on the inputs works like augmentation, and more data or a smaller model often beats them all.

"""Make a network overfit a small training set, then rein it in with L2, dropout, augmentation and early stopping."""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
from keras import layers, regularizers
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

EPOCHS = 150


def load_data():
    digits = load_digits()
    images = (digits.images.astype("float32") / 16.0)[..., None]  # (n, 8, 8, 1)
    X_rest, X_val, y_rest, y_val = train_test_split(images, digits.target, test_size=0.3, random_state=0,
                                                    stratify=digits.target)
    # Only 300 training images: a big network can memorise them
    X_train, _, y_train, _ = train_test_split(X_rest, y_rest, train_size=300, random_state=0, stratify=y_rest)
    return X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val


def build(l2=0.0, dropout=0.0, augment=False):
    reg = regularizers.L2(l2) if l2 else None
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(8, 8, 1))])
    if augment:
        # TODO: add a layers.RandomTranslation layer that shifts images by up to one pixel (1/8 of their
        #      height and width) and fills the edge with zeros (fill_mode="constant")
        pass
    model.add(layers.Flatten())
    for _ in range(2):
        model.add(layers.Dense(256, activation="relu", kernel_regularizer=reg))
        if dropout:
            # TODO: add a Dropout layer with the given rate after each hidden layer
            pass
    model.add(layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"))
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.001), loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
                  metrics=["accuracy"])
    return model


def run(name, data, callbacks=(), **settings):
    X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val = data
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    model = build(**settings)
    h = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=EPOCHS, batch_size=32, validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
                  callbacks=list(callbacks), verbose=0).history
    train_acc = model.evaluate(X_train, y_train, verbose=0)[1]
    val_acc = model.evaluate(X_val, y_val, verbose=0)[1]
    # Keras adds weight penalties to the loss it reports, so measure the plain cross-entropy for a fair comparison
    val_ce = float(np.mean(keras.losses.sparse_categorical_crossentropy(y_val, model.predict(X_val, verbose=0))))
    print(f"{name:26} epochs {len(h['loss']):3d}  train acc {train_acc:.3f}  val acc {val_acc:.3f}  "
          f"gap {train_acc - val_acc:.3f}  val cross-entropy {val_ce:.3f}")


def main():
    data = load_data()
    print("Training images", data[0].shape, "validation images", data[2].shape)
    run("baseline", data)
    run("L2 1e-3", data, l2=1e-3)
    run("L2 1e-2", data, l2=1e-2)
    run("dropout 0.5", data, dropout=0.5)
    run("augmentation (shift 1px)", data, augment=True)
    # TODO: early stopping: monitor "val_loss" with patience 10 and restore_best_weights=True (verbose=1)
    stop = None
    if stop is not None:
        run("early stopping", data, callbacks=[stop])
        run("all four together", data, callbacks=[stop], l2=1e-3, dropout=0.5, augment=True)

    model = build(dropout=0.5)
    x = data[2][:1]
    same = np.allclose(model(x, training=False), model(x, training=False))
    differ = not np.allclose(model(x, training=True), model(x, training=True))
    print(f"Dropout off at inference (same output twice): {same}; on in training (outputs differ): {differ}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: RandomTranslation(height_factor, width_factor) takes fractions of the image size: 0.125 of 8 pixels is one pixel.

modules.summary: Normalise activations inside the network: how batch normalisation computes, learns and switches between training and inference, why it lets networks train faster with higher learning rates, and where it goes wrong.

lessons.title: How batch normalisation works
objectives: Describe the batch normalisation computation and its learned scale and shift
Explain how it behaves in training and in inference
Place BatchNormalization layers in a Keras model
key_points: For each feature (each channel, in a convolutional layer), batch normalisation standardises the input with the mini-batch's mean μ_B and variance σ²_B, x̂ = (x − μ_B)/√(σ²_B + ε), then applies a learned scale and shift, y = γx̂ + β, so the network can undo the normalisation where that helps.

In training it also keeps moving averages of the mean and variance (in Keras, moving = 0.99 × moving + 0.01 × the batch's value). At inference it uses those averages instead of the batch's statistics, so a prediction doesn't depend on the other examples in the batch.

Keras's BatchNormalization(momentum=0.99, epsilon=0.001) uses batch statistics when called with training=True, as in fit(), and the moving averages with training=False, as in predict() and evaluate().
Each BatchNormalization layer holds four values per feature: γ and β are trained, while the moving mean and moving variance aren't, which is why model.summary() reports non-trainable parameters.

The original paper placed batch normalisation between a layer's weighted sum and its activation; after the activation also works. A layer followed by batch normalisation needs no bias of its own, since β does that job: Dense(64, use_bias=False).

lessons.title: Why it helps, and where it goes wrong
objectives: Explain the benefits of batch normalisation and the debate about how it works
Avoid its pitfalls with small batches, fine-tuning and shifted data
Choose layer or group normalisation when batch statistics don't suit
key_points: Ioffe and Szegedy (2015) introduced batch normalisation to reduce internal covariate shift, the change in each layer's input distribution as earlier layers learn. Later work (Santurkar et al., 2018) argued that its main effect is a smoother loss surface, so how it works is still debated.
In practice it lets networks train with higher learning rates, makes them far less sensitive to initialisation, and often reaches a given accuracy in many fewer epochs.
It also regularises slightly: each example's normalisation depends on the other examples in its batch, which adds noise, so networks with batch normalisation often need less dropout.

It struggles with very small batches, whose statistics are noisy, and when inference data differ from the training data. When fine-tuning a pre-trained model, keep its BatchNormalization layers in inference mode; in Keras, setting trainable = False on such a layer does that.

Layer normalisation normalises each example across its own features, independently of the batch, so it works with any batch size and with sequences; it's standard in transformers and recurrent networks. Group normalisation, in between, suits vision models trained with small batches.

"""Batch normalisation by hand and in Keras, then a deep network trained with and without it."""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
from keras import layers
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


def batchnorm_by_hand(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-3):
    """Normalise each column (feature) with the batch's mean and variance, then scale and shift."""
    # TODO: mean and variance of each column (axis=0, the population variance), then
    #      x_hat = (x - mean) / sqrt(var + eps) and return gamma * x_hat + beta
    return x


def by_hand_versus_keras():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    x = rng.normal(loc=5.0, scale=3.0, size=(16, 4)).astype("float32")
    bn = layers.BatchNormalization()  # momentum=0.99, epsilon=0.001 by default
    out = bn(x, training=True).numpy()
    print("Per-feature mean after BN:", out.mean(axis=0).round(3), " std:", out.std(axis=0).round(3))
    gamma, beta = bn.gamma.numpy(), bn.beta.numpy()
    print("By hand matches Keras in training mode:", bool(np.allclose(out, batchnorm_by_hand(x, gamma, beta), atol=1e-5)))
    expected = 0.99 * 0.0 + 0.01 * x.mean(axis=0)
    print("Moving mean after one batch:", bn.moving_mean.numpy().round(4), " expected:", expected.round(4))
    infer = bn(x, training=False).numpy()
    by_moving = (x - bn.moving_mean.numpy()) / np.sqrt(bn.moving_variance.numpy() + 1e-3)
    print("Inference mode uses the moving statistics:", bool(np.allclose(infer, by_moving, atol=1e-5)))


def deep_net(batchnorm):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(64,))], name="with_bn" if batchnorm else "without_bn")
    for _ in range(8):
        # TODO: for the BN version, add Dense(64, use_bias=False), then BatchNormalization, then a sigmoid
        #      Activation; otherwise add Dense(64, activation="sigmoid")
        model.add(layers.Dense(64, activation="sigmoid"))
    model.add(layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"))
    return model


def train_both():
    X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
    X = X.astype("float32") / 16.0
    X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0, stratify=y)
    for batchnorm in (False, True):
        model = deep_net(batchnorm)
        if batchnorm:
            model.summary()
        for lr in (0.01, 0.1):
            model = deep_net(batchnorm)
            model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=lr, momentum=0.9),
                          loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
            h = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=32, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), verbose=0).history
            print(f"{model.name:10} lr={lr:<5} val_accuracy after 2 epochs {h['val_accuracy'][1]:.3f}, "
                  f"after 10 {h['val_accuracy'][-1]:.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    by_hand_versus_keras()
    train_both()

hints: x.var(axis=0) is the population variance (dividing by n), which is what batch normalisation uses.
The standard deviation after BN is a little under 1 because ε = 0.001 is added to the variance.
A sigmoid network without BN learns slowly here whatever the rate: that's the vanishing gradient of Module 1 at work.

modules.title: Practical Optimisation Project
modules.summary: Bring every technique together: a dependable recipe for building and training a deep network, tuning the learning rate, batch size and schedule, reading learning curves to debug training, and a final evaluation on a hold-out test set.

lessons.title: A recipe for training a deep network
objectives: Follow a step-by-step recipe that combines initialisation, normalisation and regularisation
Run experiments that can be compared fairly
key_points: Start simple and strong: ReLU (or GELU) layers with He initialisation, batch normalisation, Adam at 0.001, a batch size of 32 to 256, and no regularisation yet; record a baseline score on the validation data first.
Before long runs, check that the network can overfit one small batch, driving its training loss close to 0. If it can't, there's a bug or too little capacity, and regularisation won't help.
Then reduce overfitting, cheapest first: more or augmented data, dropout or weight decay, early stopping, a smaller network. Tune the learning rate and its schedule as you go.
Change one thing at a time, fix the random seeds, log every run's settings and results, and repeat promising runs with a few seeds: a difference smaller than the run-to-run spread means nothing.
Keep three datasets with separate jobs: training data fits the weights, validation data chooses the settings and when to stop, and the test set is used once, at the end.

lessons.title: Tuning the learning rate, batch size and schedule
objectives: Tune the learning rate first, on a logarithmic scale
Explain how batch size and learning rate interact
Choose a schedule and a search strategy
key_points: Search learning rates on a logarithmic scale, such as 3 × 10⁻⁴, 10⁻³ and 3 × 10⁻³, rather than evenly spaced values, and tune it before other settings, because their best values depend on it.

Larger batches give less noisy gradients and use hardware better, and usually tolerate a larger learning rate; a common heuristic for SGD (Goyal et al., 2017) scales the rate in proportion to the batch size, with warm-up. Very large batches can generalise worse without such care.
Cosine decay to a small final rate, after a short warm-up, is a strong default schedule; ReduceLROnPlateau is a simple adaptive alternative when the number of epochs isn't known in advance.

Random search over several settings at once usually beats a grid of the same size, because it tries more distinct values of the settings that matter (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012); KerasTuner automates random and Bayesian search for Keras models.

lessons.title: Reading learning curves and debugging training
objectives: Diagnose underfitting, overfitting and a bad learning rate from learning curves
Run the standard sanity checks on a new network
Use TerminateOnNaN and TensorBoard while training
key_points: Check the first loss: a classifier over C balanced classes that starts out guessing uniformly reports about ln C, 2.30 for 10 classes. A much larger first loss means confident wrong outputs, often from bad initialisation or unscaled inputs.

Read the curves: both losses high and flat means underfitting (more capacity, longer training or a better learning rate); training loss falling while validation loss rises means overfitting (regularise); a jagged or rising training loss means the rate is too high; a slow, steady decline means it's too low.

NaN losses usually come from a learning rate that's too high, exploding gradients, log(0) or a division by zero; keras.callbacks.TerminateOnNaN stops training at the first NaN so the cause can be traced.

keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir="logs/run1") logs losses and metrics every epoch (and weight histograms if asked); tensorboard --logdir logs then shows several runs' curves side by side in a browser.
Evaluate the final model once on the hold-out test set and report it beside the validation score: a large gap means the settings were tuned too closely to the validation data.

"""Diagnose a badly trained network, then rescue it one change at a time."""

import math
import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
from keras import layers
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

BAD = {"activation": "sigmoid", "init": "random_normal_2", "batchnorm": False, "dropout": 0.0,
       "optimizer": "sgd_0.01", "schedule": False, "early_stopping": False}


def load_data():
    X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
    X = X.astype("float32") / 16.0
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=y)
    X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X_train, y_train, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=y_train)
    return X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test


def make_initializer(name):
    return keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=2.0) if name == "random_normal_2" else name


def make_optimizer(name, schedule, steps):
    if name == "sgd_0.01":
        return keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01)
    lr = keras.optimizers.schedules.CosineDecay(0.003, decay_steps=steps) if schedule else 0.001
    return keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=lr)


def make_model(cfg):
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(64,))])
    for _ in range(6):
        if cfg["batchnorm"]:
            model.add(layers.Dense(128, use_bias=False, kernel_initializer=make_initializer(cfg["init"])))
            model.add(layers.BatchNormalization())
            model.add(layers.Activation(cfg["activation"]))
        else:
            model.add(layers.Dense(128, activation=cfg["activation"], kernel_initializer=make_initializer(cfg["init"])))
        if cfg["dropout"]:
            model.add(layers.Dropout(cfg["dropout"]))
    # The bad initialiser is used for the output layer too; otherwise the output layer keeps Keras's default
    out_init = make_initializer(cfg["init"]) if cfg["init"] == "random_normal_2" else "glorot_uniform"
    model.add(layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax", kernel_initializer=out_init))
    return model


def diagnose(cfg, X, y):
    """Three quick checks before any long training run."""
    model = make_model(cfg)
    loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()
    # TODO: 1. the initial loss on X, y against the loss of a uniform guess, ln(10)
    # TODO: 2. each Dense layer's kernel gradient norm on this batch, first and last
    # TODO: 3. can it overfit 32 examples? Train on X[:32] for 100 epochs and report the final loss


def experiment(name, cfg, data, epochs=60):
    X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, _, _ = data
    model = make_model(cfg)
    steps = epochs * math.ceil(len(X_train) / 32)
    model.compile(optimizer=make_optimizer(cfg["optimizer"], cfg["schedule"], steps),
                  loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", metrics=["accuracy"])
    callbacks = [keras.callbacks.TerminateOnNaN()]
    if cfg["early_stopping"]:
        callbacks.append(keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=8, restore_best_weights=True))
    h = model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=epochs, batch_size=32, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), verbose=0,
                  callbacks=callbacks).history
    best = int(np.argmax(h["val_accuracy"]))
    print(f"{name:34} epochs run {len(h['loss']):2d}  best val_accuracy {h['val_accuracy'][best]:.3f} "
          f"(epoch {best + 1})  last val_loss {h['val_loss'][-1]:.3f}")
    return model


def main():
    data = load_data()
    X_train, y_train = data[0], data[1]
    print("Diagnosing the bad configuration:", BAD)
    diagnose(BAD, X_train[:256], y_train[:256])

    print("\nOne change at a time (each row keeps the changes above it)")
    steps = [
        ("bad configuration", {}),
        # TODO: add one row per fix, each a dict of changes to the configuration:
        #      ("+ ReLU and He initialisation", {"activation": "relu", "init": "he_normal"}),
        #      then Adam, batch normalisation, dropout 0.2 with early stopping, and a cosine schedule
    ]
    cfg = dict(BAD)
    model = None
    for name, change in steps:
        cfg.update(change)
        model = experiment(name, cfg, data)

    print("\nDiagnosing the final configuration:", cfg)
    diagnose(cfg, X_train[:256], y_train[:256])
    X_test, y_test = data[4], data[5]
    print(f"Final model, test accuracy (measured once): {model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=0)[1]:.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Capstone starter: a deep network that trains badly on Fashion-MNIST. Diagnose it and fix it."""

import os

os.environ.setdefault("TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL", "2")

import keras
import numpy as np
from keras import layers

CLASSES = ["T-shirt/top", "Trouser", "Pullover", "Dress", "Coat", "Sandal", "Shirt", "Sneaker", "Bag", "Ankle boot"]


def load_data(validation=10_000):
    """Fashion-MNIST: 60,000 training and 10,000 test images, 28 x 28 greyscale (about 30 MB, downloaded once)."""
    (x_train, y_train), (x_test, y_test) = keras.datasets.fashion_mnist.load_data()
    x_train, x_test = x_train.astype("float32") / 255.0, x_test.astype("float32") / 255.0
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    order = rng.permutation(len(x_train))
    val, train = order[:validation], order[validation:]
    return (x_train[train], y_train[train]), (x_train[val], y_train[val]), (x_test, y_test)


def build_bad_model():
    """Eight sigmoid layers, weights drawn far too large, and no normalisation or regularisation."""
    model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input(shape=(28, 28)), layers.Flatten()], name="bad_network")
    for _ in range(8):
        model.add(layers.Dense(256, activation="sigmoid",
                               kernel_initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=1.0)))
    model.add(layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"))
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.5), loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
                  metrics=["accuracy"])
    return model


def main():
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(0)
    (x_train, y_train), (x_val, y_val), (x_test, y_test) = load_data()
    print("train", x_train.shape, "validation", x_val.shape, "test", x_test.shape)
    model = build_bad_model()
    model.summary()
    history = model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=256, validation_data=(x_val, y_val), verbose=2)
    print(f"Best validation accuracy: {max(history.history['val_accuracy']):.3f}")
    # Keep the test set for your final, chosen model:
    # print(model.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
